limitations: Nothing here has been printed, handled or played. The fits, wall thicknesses and overhang margins are measurements taken on the exact CAD solids and predictions for a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.2 mm layers.

The verification pipeline ran for 786.91 s and FINISHED EVERY CHECK. Result: PASS, exit 0. Of its 11 steps, 7 ran and passed and three were not applicable and are recorded as not run rather than as passed -- the mounting and power checks, because there is no bought part and no powered system in this set, and the motion check, which is switched off for this build. None was left unverified. The geometry inspection completed all 51 of its checks with status 'passed' and was not interrupted, cancelled or timed out, so there is no unverified geometry to disclose: that covers validating all 224 occurrences of the assembled set, checking the whole assembly for interference, and validating all 24 printed parts individually. Of the 786.91 s, 254.48 went on regenerating every STEP from source and 514.56 on the single inspect batch. Separately, in their own rounds, all 24 printed parts cleared the 0.80 mm wall gate and the 45-degree overhang gate at a 0.4 mm nozzle: 24 of 24 PASS on each, with zero square millimetres anywhere needing support. Those gate results are measurements on the CAD solids, not a print-readiness claim, and none is sealed as one. GEOMETRY-NOTES.md carries the same record.
Motion verification is switched off for this build and is recorded as unverified rather than passed. Nothing in the set moves relative to anything else in any case.

Venus is drawn from radar, not from light. Its surface is under an opaque atmosphere, so the only picture of it is the Magellan global radar mosaic, and the rings this piece is built from are stylised silhouettes of the major highland and lowland provinces at the accuracy a 16.53 mm globe can hold -- not Magellan mapping. What they claim is that Venus has one long equatorial highland, a handful of smaller ones and three broad lowland plains; they do not claim any boundary is where the spacecraft put it. Aphrodite Terra's sweep is the one shape on the globe a reader can check against the image.

None of the reference's texture survives, and none of it is faked. The mosaic is dominated by fine filamentary radar brightness -- tesserae, lava channels, fracture belts, the ragged look of beaten gold -- and one degree of arc is 0.1443 mm on this globe while the 0.4 mm nozzle needs 2.77 degrees, so a filament a few tens of kilometres wide is about a fifth of one nozzle width. The piece carries the continents and the plains and none of the texture: it is a simplified map of the reference, not the reference. No stippling and no fine ribs stand in for it, because the set's material rules forbid deliberate grit and at this size it would print as noise.

One whole Venusian province is drawn and cannot be seen. Venus's axis is tipped 177.36 degrees, which puts the planet's north pole into the collar the globe stands in, so Ishtar Terra -- which runs from Venusian +54 to +76 -- lands entirely inside that collar on both armies, and 36 per cent of Atalanta Planitia goes the same way. Ishtar is not absent from the plastic: 3.04 mm3 of beige survives above the disc's own cut and prints inside the collar where nothing can see it, so whoever loads the printer will find a beige body with no picture on it. Neither province was dropped and neither is a fault: the reason they are invisible is the inversion the set carries on purpose. cad/measure/venus-atlas-resolution.md measures it province by province.

Venus's beige highlands separate only 20.2 of 255 greyscale levels from its sunflower-yellow globe in the canonical renders -- the thinnest marking separation anywhere in this set, and below the 21.8 this set rejected on Mercury as invisible. It reads here for two measured reasons rather than one hoped-for one: Aphrodite Terra is a single continuous marking 117 degrees of longitude wide, 16.9 mm of arc and the longest in the set, and beige is a pink-cream against an amber so the boundary carries a hue step that greyscale does not count. A smaller feature in that pair of filaments would not read. White separates 27.9 and was measured and not taken, because white is already the brightest feature on Earth, Mars and Mercury. cad/measure/venus-tone-separation.md is the measurement.

Venus's globe and Saturn's are now neighbours in hue -- sunflower yellow #FFB549 against yellow #FFD834, 23.5 greyscale levels apart sealed and 11.2 as the renders show them. They are told apart by everything except colour: 9.47 mm of globe diameter, a 30 mm ring on one and nothing of the kind on the other, and the numerals 3 and 7. Rendered side by side at the product's own frame the silhouette carries it easily and the colour alone would not. cad/measure/venus-saturn-separation.md is that check.

Venus's globe also now shares sunflower yellow with the Sol star. That is stated rather than accidental: the amber was preferred to a new spool precisely because the set already carried it, and the two are never confused -- the star is a 36 mm square plinth lying flat on the board with two 18 mm flames rising off it.

Venus's four small highlands -- Alpha, Themis, Beta and Phoebe Regio -- are six-vertex rings 15 to 20 degrees across and read as small polygons at this size rather than as landforms. All four clear the nozzle, at 0.66 to 1.12 mm at their narrowest against a 0.40 mm floor, so none was dropped, none was shrunk to a dot and none was replaced by a circle.

Venus is one of the worlds that takes three filaments -- sunflower yellow, beige and cocoa brown -- where it used to take two. No new spool is needed: all three were already loaded for this set. Earth takes four; Mercury, Mars, Venus, Neptune, Saturn and Jupiter take three; Uranus alone takes two.

Aphrodite Terra spans more than 150 degrees of longitude, which is past the 72-degree limit of the outline tool that sweeps a ring into the globe, so the build draws it as two rings overlapping across 28 degrees whose union is the drawn ring exactly. No vertex moved and no width changed, and the built solids confirm the two come out as one continuous highland rather than two.

Mercury is the other world in the set that takes three filaments -- grey, cocoa brown and white. On this 13.78 mm globe the dark grey the plains used to carry is 21.8 of 255 greyscale levels away from the grey globe it sits on, and at that separation the patches are simply not visible. Cocoa brown measures 45.5 on the same test and the basin's white floor 36.9 against the globe and 114.3 against the rim. Black separates furthest at 139.6 and was deliberately not used: a black patch on a small grey ball reads as a hole in the print rather than as terrain.

Cocoa brown is a warm brown rather than a neutral grey, so at a glance Mercury's plains and Venus's lowlands sit in the same family of colour as Mars's dark continents and Saturn's and Jupiter's bands. That is the price of the separations above and it was paid deliberately.

Mercury's plains are drawn from a formula rather than from a map. Its albedo boundaries are genuinely soft and its plains are genuinely unnamed, so there is no silhouette anyone could check the model against. The Caloris basin's size and latitude are real; its longitude is a camera decision and is stated as one.

No crater field was added to Mercury, Mars or Venus. On each of the three the largest crater outside a named basin is one or two nozzle widths across, with no room for a rim and a floor inside it, so it would print as a pit one extrusion wide and read as a print defect. Caloris is the exception precisely because at 36 degrees of arc it is eleven nozzle widths across.

Mars's dark markings are the classical albedo map at the accuracy an eyepiece sketch has, not spacecraft mapping. Four vertices were moved to clear the nozzle; none of them moves an outline the eye reads. Mars's albedo is cocoa brown on a red globe, and those two filaments are only 1.88:1 apart in contrast -- under the 3:1 at which a difference in value reads as darkness rather than as a change of colour.

Mars's globe is sunk 2.00 mm into its disc and cut level with it, which at Mars's axial tilt removes about a seventh of the sphere and almost all of the south polar cap. The northern cap is the larger and more irregular of the two and that is measurable in the geometry, but it is not visible on the finished piece and is not claimed to be.

Earth's coastlines are a stylised silhouette atlas, not a survey coastline. Central America is one broad land bridge, and Japan, New Zealand, the Indonesian and Philippine arcs, the British Isles as a shape of their own, the Mediterranean's islands and Antarctica are not drawn; most are narrower than a 0.4 mm nozzle on a 16.70 mm globe, and each is listed with its reason in cad/measure/earth-atlas-resolution.md. One vertex was moved: the Australian outback's north-west corner came 0.33 mm inland. Nothing was dropped silently.

Earth's beige dryland is #F7E6DE, a very pale warm white. At this globe size it sits close in value to the white ice and an unprimed reader of the renders calls it light grey rather than sand. Both filaments were required to stay, so this is stated rather than fixed.

Earth and Neptune share the same blue filament -- they are the only two worlds in the set printed from one spool. This revision changed Neptune's surface, so the pair was measured again rather than inherited: cad/measure/neptune-earth-separation.md renders the two side by side at the product's own frame and answers on size, colour, silhouette and surface separately. Colour separates them by exactly nothing and cannot be asked to. Size does the work -- 5.19 mm of globe diameter, 31 per cent, and 5.19 mm of piece height -- and surface confirms it. An independent reader shown the pair cold, before knowing the requirement: 'not even close -- instantly two different things ... Size does the work first here, and pattern confirms it.'
The low side of Saturn's ring is thickened where its underside is carried down to the disc. That is what lets a tilted ring print without support, and it is visible from a seated eye.

The star's two flames are slimmer than the design that was handed in. The feet were narrowed to 6.00 mm and brought inboard so each flame stands on solid flange and prints without support; their 18 mm height, their outward lean and their taper are unchanged.

The review renders under cad/snap/ are drawn by a tool that encodes colour twice, so in those images every mid-tone is lifted: Mars's and Venus's cocoa brown appears as a light ochre and Venus's amber globe appears paler than the filament is. The colours sealed on the parts themselves are the catalogue values and are what a printer and a listing read. cad/measure/filament-value.md measures both ends of it. Every visual judgement in this build, the blind review included, was made on those double-encoded images; that is a limitation of this build's evidence.

The renders are flat-shaded with no ground plane and no shadows. A black disc comes out as a featureless silhouette, the two storage trays read as floating because nothing under them is drawn, and the seven-segment numerals sit on the disc wall facing the two seated players, so at the product's own oblique frame they are turned nearly side-on and cannot be read. All of that is the renderer rather than the solids; the numerals read correctly in the per-world frames under cad/snap/worlds/.

Uranus was corrected by the PREVIOUS revision and is not reopened here. Its one white equatorial band -- the last closed band left on any world in the set at that point -- was replaced by a polar hood at each pole and by an upright ring, and every Uranus constant is exactly where that revision left it. This revision touches only Neptune, and it puts a closed band system BACK, which is the opposite direction to the change Uranus was given. That is not a contradiction: Uranus's band was wrong for Uranus because a planet lying on its side shows a polar hood rather than an equatorial belt, and it stood upright on the visible face. Neptune's bands are not wrong for Neptune; the owner simply prefers them to the short arcs that replaced them.

This set is not published by this run and carries no published name. Antisol Poseidon is a working title for an unpublished revision of the unpublished set the previous revisions produced, and this run carries --no-publish. Whether and under what name the set is published is decided after the whole owner's-second-pass seals. The archive for this revision lands at toys/ad-astra-antisol-poseidon.

Recorded by the PREVIOUS revision's independent reviewer, about Venus, and carried forward rather than dropped; it is not evidence from this run's review. An independent reviewer of this build's images disagrees with one choice the correction brief made, and the disagreement is recorded rather than buried. In their words: the Magellan reference's bright highland terrain measures hue 38 degrees at saturation 0.66 against a ground of hue 30 at 0.83, so on the real planet the bright terrain is warmer and yellower than the ground it sits on; beige #F7E6DE is hue 19 at saturation 0.10 against a globe of #FFB549 at hue 36, so the piece's bright tone is pinker and cooler than its globe. The hue relationship is inverted relative to the reference. The brief names beige, so this build kept it. cad/measure/venus-highland-palette.md checks all nineteen stocked filaments and finds only one that is brighter than the globe, warm and chromatic -- yellow #FFD834 -- which separates 9.6 greyscale levels from the globe in the canonical render against beige's 20.2, the weakest marking separation in the set, and which is Saturn's own globe filament. The objection is a real limit of the filament range and cannot be fixed with the plastics this shop stocks.

Recorded by the PREVIOUS revision's independent reviewer, about Venus, and carried forward rather than dropped; it is not evidence from this run's review. Asked directly whether the piece reads as the same planet as the Magellan reference, that reviewer answered no on the Aphrodite face and arguable on the other. They could match the three-tone scheme, the amber ground hue, an elongated bright feature crossing the equatorial zone and dark blotches at middle latitudes. They could not find, and the piece does not carry: the reference's reticulated mesh of branching bright threads, its saturation, its dark terrain as a major constituent, any radiating streak or linear ridge, and any circular corona or impact basin. That is the expected outcome and the brief says so in advance -- the piece is a simplified map of the reference, not the reference.

At the hero framing Venus's globe is 211 pixels across and the lowland occupies 2.8 per cent of it, a single dark smudge at the collar, while the highland occupies 14.9 per cent, so a buyer looking at the hero image sees one marking on Venus. This follows from the planet's geography rather than from the framing: sweeping the single-piece camera through 360 degrees, Aphrodite peaks at 1.00 on the visibility index with the plains at 0.44, and the plains peak at 2.00 with Aphrodite at 0.21. No camera shows both, because Venus's major plains lie on the hemisphere away from Aphrodite. cad/measure/venus-facing.md is that sweep.

On the Aphrodite face -- three of the eight product images -- the lone cocoa wedge reads as a stray polygon rather than as terrain, because it is the only dark marking present, it is clipped flat where the globe enters its collar, and it has no neighbours to belong to. The same material on the opposite face reads immediately as terrain. The clipping is correct behaviour, not a modelling fault.

Aphrodite Terra spans roughly half the globe's circumference rather than most of it: measuring the near-limb annulus degree by degree in the overhead frame, highland occupies 25 per cent of it in four separate arcs, the longest 53 degrees. That follows from the supplied ring data rather than from the build.

In the hero frame Venus's highland band, Saturn's ring, Saturn's new northern cap and both piece bases read as the same near-white, so the frame's brightest elements are one tone. The pieces remain easy to tell apart by size and by Saturn's ring.

Jupiter's zones are a bright cream rather than a white, and the filament is beige #F7E6DE -- the same spool Earth's dry interiors and Venus's highlands already use. On the renders it reads as a very pale warm white and an unprimed reader may call it white rather than cream. White #FFFEF7 measured further from the orange globe and was not taken, because it is already the brightest feature on four other worlds here and because the reference's zones are cream. cad/measure/jupiter-tone-separation.md is the measurement and carries the number that choice cost.

The wave on Jupiter's two widest belt boundaries is a designed irregularity, not Jovian data. It is two harmonics of longitude summing to 2.5 degrees of arc on each boundary, chosen to take the lathe look off an exact circle of latitude. It does not correspond to any feature on the real planet, and the four narrower belts do not carry it at all -- at 5 to 7 degrees wide the same wave would close them.

The Great Red Spot's collar and the South Temperate Belt meet. The spot is 9 degrees of arc tall centred at latitude -22 and the South Tropical Zone it sits in is 7 degrees deep, so a collar wide enough to print at all -- 2.00 degrees, 0.47 mm, 1.2 nozzle widths -- reaches past -27 into that belt. Rather than bite a second hollow out of a belt this correction requires to stay a plain circle of latitude, the collar gives way there, and over 11.7 degrees of longitude, 2.56 mm of arc, the two are one continuous cocoa-brown region. Both are the same filament, so nothing prints differently; what a reader sees is the spot's collar touching the belt below it.

Jupiter's poles are bare globe above latitude +46 and below -46, with the last belt ending at +43. That is deliberate: the reference darkens toward the poles rather than brightening, and bare orange is closer to that than a bright zone would be. At the piece's own pole frame the result is a large plain orange cap with the belt system ringing it.

None of the reference's fine detail survives on Jupiter, and none of it is faked. The white ovals in the temperate belts subtend 2 to 4 degrees of arc, which is one to two nozzle widths with no room for a colour boundary either side; the festoons hanging off the North Equatorial Belt are under a degree wide, and the filamentary turbulence along every belt edge is finer again. One degree of arc is 0.2354 mm on this 26.97 mm globe and the 0.4 mm nozzle is 1.70 degrees of it. No stippling and no fine ribs stand in for them.

Jupiter now takes four filaments -- orange, cocoa brown, beige and red -- where it took three, which ties it with Earth as the most expensive world in the set. No new spool is needed: all four were already loaded.

Jupiter's five bright zones are inlaid 1.14 mm deep rather than the 1.20 mm the belts, the spot and its collar reach. The 0.06 mm of clearance -- under a third of one 0.2 mm layer, and buried under the globe's surface where nothing can see it -- keeps the zones' floor off the sphere the outline markings bottom out on. Built at equal depth the two floors are one surface described twice, and the boolean left a 0.03 mm3 shard of bare globe floating six micrometres under the surface, different on the two armies. Measured, not assumed; cad/parts/jupiter_atlas.py carries the number.

A band marking in this set is a lens that reaches its full depth at its own middle and tapers to nothing at its own edges, so the last fraction of a degree of each of Jupiter's four plain belts -- and of Saturn's belts, Neptune's streaks and Uranus's band -- is a skin thinner than one 0.2 mm layer. That is how every band marking here has always been built. It is a depth rather than a width: every colour boundary the nozzle has to lay down is measured in cad/measure/jupiter-atlas-resolution.md and none of them is under 0.4 mm.

Each of Jupiter's bright zones stops at the exact latitude of the plain belt beside it, not a fraction of a degree past it, and that zero was measured rather than chosen. A band marking in this set tapers to nothing at its own edge, so a zone drawn past one runs underneath the belt's feather at full depth instead of being trimmed by it. Drawn a whole degree past, that buried beige cut the orange globe into three separate solids. Drawn a quarter of a degree past, the globe stayed whole but the two bodies interlocked along the feather's knife edge and the interference gate could not answer the pair -- it reported the South Temperate Belt's entire 51.52 mm3 as a clash with the South Tropical Zone on the Anti-Sol world and nothing at all on the Sol world, from geometry that is its mirror. Drawn to the exact latitude the gate is clean on both armies, and the fifteen colour bodies of one world sum to the printed solid within 0.000008 mm3.

Saturn was corrected by the PREVIOUS revision and is not reopened here; it is the world that revision corrected, and it is the only correction in the chain that lowers a world's contrast instead of raising it. It wore four cocoa-brown bands each exactly 12 degrees wide at -51/-39, -21/-9, 9/21 and 39/51 -- equal width, equal spacing, mirror-symmetric -- in the highest-contrast pairing the palette offers. It now wears five bands at 9, 15, 8, 16 and 12 degrees, unevenly spaced and not symmetric about the equator, four of them sunflower yellow and only the widest still cocoa brown, plus a bright white cap above 58 degrees north. Saturn's ring system is not part of the correction and did not move: every value in its block of params.py is the one the published set had, and because the ring is a solid rather than an inlay it is compared on solid count, exact volume and bounding box in cad/measure/occurrence-geometry.md rather than on colour.

Saturn's light bands separate only 9.4 of 255 greyscale levels from its globe in the canonical renders. That is the smallest marking separation this project has committed to -- smaller than the 20.2 it calls its thinnest, on Venus, and smaller than the 21.8 it once rejected on Mercury as invisible -- and it is stated as a number rather than called clear. It is the intended result: the reference is the softest image in the set and this world is meant to be the quiet one beside Jupiter's loud one. It reads for two measured reasons, area and hue: the bands cover about 102,000 pixels of a 900-pixel frame where Mercury's vanished patches were a few millimetres across, and an amber against a green-yellow carries a change of hue that a greyscale number does not count. The fallback tone the brief allowed, beige, measured 10.1 -- seven tenths of a level better, which is not a difference -- and was not taken. cad/measure/saturn-tone-separation.md is the measurement.

Saturn's band edges cannot be soft and the reference's are. A flush colour inlay changes colour at a line; the reference's bands fade into one another. Lowering the contrast is the available substitute for softening the edge, and it is a substitute rather than a cure. The 2.5-degree wave on the two widest bands takes the lathe look off those two boundaries and does nothing for the other six.

Saturn's bright northern cap is on the north only, so it is in plain view on the Sol piece and nearly gone on the Anti-Sol one -- 29,333 pixels against 8,882 at the product's own frame, which is a crescent along the upper limb rather than a region on the face of the ball. That is the 26.73-degree lean the two armies already differ by and it is intended, not a mirror failure; the two pieces carry the same cap and each piece's own polar frame shows it at 42,908 and 41,874 pixels. It is never hidden completely at any frame the product is photographed from. cad/measure/saturn-cap-visibility.md measures all of it.

The two Saturn pieces are not identical in volume everywhere, and the difference is named rather than rounded away. Ring, cap and the four light bands agree to 7.1e-05, 1.4e-03 and 9.6e-04 mm3, but the globe and the one dark band differ by 0.103 and 0.074 mm3 -- 0.0012 and 0.0248 per cent of themselves. The cause is measured: the globe is cut flat where it enters its disc, at piece latitude -57.80 degrees, so a marking is buried by the disc wherever it reaches below planet latitude -31.07 at the meridian the piece leans along, and that meridian is longitude 0 on the Sol piece and longitude 180 on the Anti-Sol one. The widest band's wavy south boundary stands at -30.51 on one and -32.48 on the other, so the Anti-Sol piece buries a little more of it inside its own base. Nothing above the seat line differs. Narrowing that wave until it cleared the line on both meridians would have been a visible change made to hide an invisible one.

Saturn's band amber is the same sunflower yellow that is Venus's entire globe, so from this run the two pieces are built out of the same two spools where before they shared only cocoa brown. Measured after the change rather than before it, at the product's own frame: size and silhouette tell them apart easily -- 9.47 mm of globe diameter, Saturn 36 per cent the taller in pixels, and a ring Venus has nothing like -- and the surface does not. The surface is the weakest of the three cues and this correction made it weaker. What still separates them there is which way round the colours sit: Venus is a flat amber ball with one pale province, Saturn a lighter gold ball wearing the amber as soft stripes under a white cap. cad/measure/venus-saturn-separation.md is that check and it is not rounded up.

Saturn's five band latitudes are a reading of ref/saturn-sol.png rather than Saturnian data, and the 2.5 degrees of wave on the two widest boundaries corresponds to no feature on the planet. What the piece claims is that Saturn's bands are wide, unequal, unevenly spaced, not symmetric about its equator and low in contrast, and that its northern third is lighter than its southern. It does not claim any boundary is where a particular image put it.

Nothing else Saturn shows is on this globe, and each omission has arithmetic behind it rather than taste. No hexagonal polar vortex: it is real and it is at the pole this piece is looked at from, it spans 28.5 degrees of arc or 6.47 mm so the figure would fit, but its visible edge is a jet-stream boundary 0.11 mm wide at the most generous reading -- a quarter of one nozzle width, against a nozzle that needs 1.76 degrees or 1,792 km -- so printed at all it would be four times too fat and would read as a moulding line round the pole. No polar vortex eye, finer again. No Great White Spot storms, which appear once a Saturnian year and are not what the reference shows. No ring spokes, which are transient shadowing rather than material. No ring divisions: the printed ring projects 2.00 mm past the globe and that stands for 62,117 km of real ring, so the Cassini division would be 0.15 mm and the Encke gap 0.010 mm. And no shadow of the ring on the globe, which is light rather than material and printed would become a permanent dark band -- the opposite of what this correction exists to produce. None of them is faked with stippling or ribs.

Saturn now prints in four filaments -- yellow, sunflower yellow, cocoa brown and white -- where it printed in three. No new spool: all four were already loaded for this set. The tightest gap on the globe is the 3 degrees, 0.68 mm, between the northernmost band and the cap above it, which is 1.7 nozzle widths of bare globe; every band width, ring edge and neck is measured against the 0.4 mm nozzle in cad/measure/saturn-atlas-resolution.md.

One thing the ring-plane frame shows that no other frame does, disclosed rather than repaired. cad/snap/worlds/saturn-<side>-ringplane.png puts the camera exactly in the plane of the ring, which is what shows the ring is a flat annulus of one thickness and what puts its support web in plain view. At that camera the ring's top face renders as a dashed row of near-zero-height slivers. The independent reviewer flagged it first as coincident surfaces z-fighting and then re-classified it as grazing-incidence aliasing; both were tested. Lifting the camera three degrees out of the ring plane does not remove it, and re-tessellating the same piece at 0.10, 0.03 and 0.008 radians of angular tolerance gives a pixel-identical pattern, so it is neither aliasing nor tessellation: it is the 96 ruled sectors of the support web meeting the ring plate's true cylinder. That is unchanged published geometry -- the ring occurrence is identical to the published set in solid count, exact volume and bounding box -- it is invisible at the product's own camera and at board scale, and it does not affect the print gates, which pass. It is left alone because repairing it would mean moving the ring, which this correction is forbidden to do.

The ring plate's own white sits directly against the globe all the way round the equator, because the plate's bore is 1.00 mm inside the globe's radius. That is the largest value step on the piece after the numeral and it is what reads the ring as a separate object rather than as a flange of the ball. The new northern cap is the same white, so the brightest thing at the top of the globe and the brightest thing across its middle are one filament -- which is what the reference shows, where the ring and the northern globe are the same cream.

Neptune's faint darker spot centre is not drawn. The reference shows the Great Dark Spot with a slightly darker core; drawing it would need a fourth filament on a globe this set holds to three, and the core's own boundary is under one nozzle width at this globe size in any case. An independent reader confirmed the omission on a four-times magnification of the shipped frame: the ellipse is 'one flat uniform mid-grey, edge to edge, with a one-pixel hard boundary and no internal structure at all'.

The two Neptune pieces are mirrors in the way this set defines one -- same ball, same markings, obliquity mirrored at +28.32 against -28.32 degrees, and the disc drafted the opposite way. On this revision the disc is the ONLY difference between them: all three white bands and the dark spot come out at exactly the same volume on both armies, to a ten-thousandth of a cubic millimetre, because a closed latitude band is a surface of revolution about the globe's own polar axis and the mirror maps each band onto itself. The build this revision corrects could not say that: two of its eight cloud streaks reached far enough south to be clipped by the disc on one army and not the other, costing 12.98 mm3 of white. cad/measure/neptune-mirror.md carries both.

An independent reader of THIS run's review renders reported that Neptune's white bands are 'raised ribs' with 'a bright lit upper edge and a grey shaded lower edge', and that its dark spot by contrast is 'paint or a decal' -- two different kinds of feature. Both claims are false and were answered by measuring the solids rather than by arguing. On both armies, every point of the bands body and every point of the spot body lies at 10.945000 mm from the globe centre against a globe radius of 10.945000 mm: proud by +0.000000 mm. They are the same kind of feature, a flush colour inlay through the outer 1.20 mm of the same ball, differing only in filament. Shown the measurement the critic withdrew the claim in writing -- 'I withdraw that entirely' -- and diagnosed the cause itself: the band bodies are near-white, so they carry the sphere's own lighting gradient across their width far more strongly than the blue does. cad/measure/neptune-flush.md is the measurement.

Uranus's globe colour is wrong against its reference and cannot be made right inside this correction. cad/ref/uranus-sol.png is a pale desaturated ice blue -- its ball means 161, 200, 206 -- and the filament is cyan #00FFFF, a saturated neon with no red in it at all. The thirteen filaments this set stocks are the supplier's entire Bambu Lab PLA Lite range and none of them is a pale blue; the only other blue-family colour is #004EA8, a dark navy, further from the reference than cyan is, and the one pale-ish blue the supplier lists at all, misty blue #688197, is a PETG Basic colour and a mid slate rather than an ice blue. A paler marking on a neon globe does not make the globe paler and none was attempted. Acquiring a pale blue is a recommendation for a future revision rather than an action here: cyan is shared with the Anti-Sol flames and the Anti-Sol corona cells, so changing it reaches well outside two printed parts. cad/measure/uranus-reference.md and cad/measure/uranus-tone-separation.md.

Uranus's ring is an owner instruction and not a reference match, and it is recorded as exactly that. cad/ref/uranus-sol.png shows no ring, and every other requirement in this chain forbids inventing what the reference does not show; this one is an explicit owner decision that overruled an earlier version of its own brief. It is defensible on its own terms -- Uranus has thirteen narrow rings, too faint for the reference image to carry -- and none of the real system is drawn: at 0.1922 mm per degree of arc the rings, the shepherd gaps and the named ringlets would all be grit under a 0.4 mm nozzle, so the piece carries one solid hoop. No moons, no storms, no banding. cad/measure/uranus-ring.md.

Uranus's hood boundary is a hard edge where the reference's is soft, for the reason every marking in this set has a hard edge: a flush colour inlay changes colour at a line, and the narrowest line a 0.4 mm nozzle lays is 2.08 degrees of arc on this 22.02 mm globe. The reference's brightening fades out and this one stops. Lowering the contrast is the substitute rather than the cure, and the tone was measured against the globe rather than picked: beige separates 29.0 of 255 luma levels from cyan and the white it replaces separates 35.2, so the tone change on its own is about a fifth quieter. What stops the piece reading as a tennis ball is the shape, not the tone. cad/measure/uranus-atlas-resolution.md.

A hood at each pole makes Uranus's surface symmetric, so at the two frames this set is photographed from the two armies show the same face. Saturn's single northern cap is an ownership cue in its own right and Uranus gives that up; it gives it up because a northern hood alone is not a cue here but a marking one army never shows. The disc in white against black, the numeral in the other tone, and the hoop's own lean still separate the two armies. cad/measure/uranus-facing.md.

The two places where Uranus's hoop leaves the disc top carry a small wedge rather than meeting it cleanly. An upright hoop this small meets the flat cut at the disc top on the steep part of its own curve -- 48.6 degrees from vertical, past the 45 the printer holds unaided, and it does not clear the gate until half a millimetre higher. Growing the ring until the cut lands shallower takes the projection back to Saturn's own 2.00 mm, so the junction is wedged instead at the 47.2 degree slope this set already trusts under Saturn's ring. The wedge stands 1.30 mm proud of the hoop at the disc top and is gone 1.50 mm higher, inside the globe; it is visible on close inspection as a small gusset at each foot. The steepest downward-facing angle anywhere on the finished hoop is then 44.3 degrees, at Z 5.68 and plan radius 8.66. cad/measure/uranus-ring.md. An independent reviewer reading the renders called that junction 'sawn off' rather than supported, across three passes, and that reading is recorded rather than argued with: the hoop does end in a blunt square cut where it meets the disc, because the set cuts every ring at the disc top. It is a structurally sound joint -- the part builds as one solid and the overhang gate passes at 44.3 degrees -- and it is not a pretty one.

Uranus still prints in two filaments -- cyan for the globe and beige for the hoods -- because its new ring prints in the globe's own cyan rather than in white. That was measured rather than inherited: a white ring separates 38.9 of 255 luma levels from this globe, louder than the hood's 27.8, and an independent reviewer shown only the images named both Uranus pieces as tennis balls on exactly that cue. Grey was tried and read as a MORE convincing seam, because a tennis seam is a dark curve on a bright ball. In the globe's own filament the hoop stops being a marking and becomes relief. No new spool is loaded and the set still prints in the same thirteen. cad/measure/uranus-ring.md.

The PREVIOUS revision was the first in this chain whose two corrected printed parts were expected to CHANGE in bytes rather than stay identical, because a ring is added material. This revision is back to the normal case and expected the opposite: a marking is a flush colour inlay, so it partitions the globe's volume without moving the printed solid's boundary, and both Neptune parts came out byte-identical to the published set's. If either hash had moved, something had moved the ball's own surface and it would have had to be found. cad/measure/revision-part-hashes.md is that check.

Three of this set's own sealed reports still describe Uranus's superseded band or count it as a two-filament world -- cad/measure/jupiter-atlas-resolution.md, cad/measure/jupiter-tone-separation.md and cad/measure/venus-tone-separation.md -- and a fourth, cad/measure/neptune-atlas-resolution.md, states Saturn's band system as 3.63 to 7.26 mm where Saturn's own report measures the narrowest band at 1.82 mm, a factor of two from taking millimetres per degree as pi*d/180 instead of pi*d/360. Those are the sealed records of earlier corrections and this set's convention is to leave each run's own record as it stands rather than back-date it. Both disagreements are named in cad/measure/uranus-atlas-resolution.md and the figures as they now stand are there and in README.md; nothing in this run depends on either.

Uranus's polar hood has no counterpart in cad/ref/uranus-sol.png. The reference shows one very faint soft-edged lighter region and no cap; the hood is the feature the planet actually carries, which is why the correction asked for it, but it is drawn harder and larger than anything in the reference and an independent reviewer flagged it at every pass. After the hood was narrowed from 55 to 60 degrees of latitude it covers about a fifth of the visible face rather than about a third; the same reviewer then reported that it reads at board scale as a stuck-on disc rather than as a brightening. A flush colour inlay cannot fade out, so that is the closest this palette and this process can get.

Two independent review passes called both Uranus pieces tennis balls before the ring colour was changed, and the third pass reported the reading gone. That sequence is recorded here rather than summarised away, because the first two passes are the evidence that the measurement alone was not enough: the tone numbers never predicted the reading, and what fixed it was moving the ring out of the marking category entirely.

Neptune's three closed white latitude bands are back in place of the eight short cloud streaks, and that is an OWNER DECISION ON APPEARANCE taken against a measured argument that is still in the archive. cad/ref/neptune-sol.png shows clouds that are SHORT -- each starts and stops inside a few tens of degrees of longitude and not one of them rings the planet -- and the run that drew the streaks made that case at length and had it confirmed by an independent blind reader. The owner has looked at both drawings and prefers the bands. The losing case is preserved word for word in cad/parts/markings.py and at item 22 of the design contract, headed by what happened to it; item 24 records the reversal. This piece does not look like its reference and is not trying to.

IT READS AS A BEACH BALL, AND IT WAS NOT ADJUSTED TO STOP IT. A closed latitude band runs the whole way round the planet, and three of them on a blue globe is what the previous edition called the most beach-ball-like object in the set. That judgement was not wrong; it was overruled. This run's independent critic was asked the question cold, in its first round, before it knew what the object was or that the question mattered, and answered: 'Yes, one piece, in both its copies. The medium-blue ball with thin pale stripes ... Both read to me as a beach ball rather than a tennis ball.' No other piece in the set drew the reading. Told afterwards that the owner had been warned and chose it anyway, it did not move. The bands were not softened, moved, narrowed or broken to make the answer come out nicer.

What actually causes that reading, diagnosed by the same critic once it had seen the reference, because this is the sentence the owner acts on: it is NOT the axial tilt and NOT the fact that there are three bands. The reference carries markings at the same latitudes and the same lean and does not read as a beach ball at all. It is three surface properties the reference does not share -- a one-pixel hard edge where the reference's clouds are feathered; a constant width of about 4 per cent of the ball's diameter where the reference's vary and some are hairline; and near-white on saturated blue where the reference's clouds are only 15 to 20 per cent brighter than their own globe. The tilt is the ownership cue and cannot be given up. If a future edition wants to move this reading without giving up closed bands, contrast is where the room is.

The bright companion cloud beside Neptune's dark spot is not drawn, and that is a deliberate loss rather than an oversight. The reference does show one and the build this revision corrects drew one; it was white, and a marking in this set is keyed by its filament, so it was one of the nine bodies of the marking that went back to three bands, and the drawing being reverted to had no companion. RECOMMENDATION, made rather than quietly dropped: it could survive as a fourth white region of its own at no cost in filament and no cost to the three bands, and a future edition should consider it.

Neptune's southernmost band, at -46/-41, cannot be seen on the Sol army at either of the two frames the set is photographed from. The Sol piece leans its north pole toward the lens, so both cameras look down on the northern hemisphere -- the state-sheet sub-point sits at +51.5 -- and at the +0.30 facing floor no marking south of about -21 can reach them at any longitude. It measures +0.23 at the Sol hero frame and -0.04 at the Sol state sheet, which is behind the limb. On the Anti-Sol army it measures +0.70 and +0.58 and is plainly visible, and at the two level per-world frames it is visible on both pieces. Moving the band is the one thing this revision was told not to do. cad/measure/neptune-facing.md measures all six cameras.

A FALSE CLAIM THIS CHAIN SEALED, CORRECTED HERE. The archived cad/measure/neptune-atlas-resolution.md said this set's other band systems are '3.63 to 7.26 mm (Saturn) and 2.35 to 6.12 mm (Jupiter)' and concluded that Neptune's markings were 'the narrowest marking family anywhere in the set'. Both figures carry a pi*d/180 doubling -- one degree of great-circle arc is pi*d/360, and on this globe that is 0.1910 mm, not 0.3821. Saturn's own report measures its narrowest band at 1.82 mm and Jupiter's its narrowest belt at 1.18 and narrowest zone at 1.06; 3.63 is exactly twice 1.82 and 2.35 exactly twice 1.18. The conclusion was false even at the corrected numbers, because the streaks it described, at 1.35-1.65 mm, were WIDER than Jupiter's narrowest zone. The rewritten report reads those three figures out of the two source reports at run time rather than copying them. Neptune's bands at 0.955, 0.764 and 0.573 mm are now the narrowest band family in the set by a factor of 1.85 -- though not the narrowest marking of any kind, since Earth's outback boundary leaves a 0.40 mm strip of green, exactly one nozzle.

Neptune's three band latitudes and widths are the ones the build carried before the cloud correction, restored verbatim, and they are a design rather than Neptunian data. They were read back off the source's own record of what it replaced -- the comment in cad/parts/markings.py quoting them as -46/-41, 11/15 and 30/33 -- rather than off the revision brief, and the two agreed. What the piece claims about Neptune's clouds is only that they are white, that there are three of them, that they are unequal in width and unevenly spaced, and that the widest is in the southern mid-latitudes. It does not claim they are the shape the reference shows.

The reference images this set is measured against are not astronomical photographs. This run's independent critic noticed it unprompted on being shown cad/ref/neptune-sol.png for the first time: 'It is a photograph or photoreal render of a finished physical piece of this same product -- the same blue ball on the same white cylindrical plinth, with a clean upright 5 on the rim, and fine horizontal FDM print layer lines across the whole surface.' That is correct and it is what the design contract already says -- twenty of the twenty-one reference images are the sealed AI-generated set, and only cad/ref/venus-radar-surface.png is a supplied photographic dataset image. It is repeated here because the cloud correction this revision reverses argued from that image, and a reader should know what kind of image it is.

Three findings from this run's independent critic stand as observations about parts this revision did not touch and could not touch, kept rather than dropped. Uranus does not self-identify: the critic failed to name it blind and said so plainly, and its geometry is right -- a 98-degree tilt is what puts a pole on the limb -- but correctness is not legibility. Mercury and Venus carry almost no information, one orange patch and one pale band, and the critic could name neither blind. And Uranus's ring meets its globe in a visible silhouette step at the top and vanishes into the collar at the lower left. None is a defect of this revision and none was repaired here.

One design observation from this run's critic that is not a defect and is worth carrying forward: the fifth-root size ladder makes rank visible END TO END and invisible BETWEEN NEIGHBOURS. Jupiter against Mercury is 1.957:1 and reads instantly; Uranus against Neptune is 0.6 per cent and Venus against Earth 0.8 per cent, which no reader can adjudicate by eye. In Dou Shou Qi, neighbours are precisely where rank has to be read. The critic also noted that mirroring each planet's own obliquity separates the armies only where that obliquity is substantial -- it works on Earth, Mars, Saturn and Neptune and does almost nothing on Jupiter at 3.13 degrees or Mercury at 0.03 -- so disc colour carries the ownership cue on those pieces.
product.summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases say it again in white against black. Four of the eight wear a real map -- Earth its coastlines, Mars its dark continents, Mercury its smooth plains with the Caloris basin in them, and Venus the radar surface no eye has seen. The other four wear their weather. Neptune is the world this edition changes, and the change is unusual enough to say at the top: nothing was wrong with it. The owner prefers the older drawing. Neptune wore three closed white bands of latitude; the edition before last replaced them with eight short tapered cloud streaks and a bright companion wisp, and argued it from Neptune's own photograph, which shows clouds that are short and do not ring the planet. That case was measured and reviewed blind. The owner has looked at both and wants the three bands back, so they are back: white, at 46 to 41 degrees south, 11 to 15 north and 30 to 33 north -- the narrowest band system in the box. The argument they overruled is kept word for word in the source that draws this world, under a heading saying what happened to it, so a reader can see both. The Great Dark Spot does not move, and that was checked on the built solids rather than assumed. The bright cloud beside it is gone with the streaks, which is a loss and is recorded as one. Both Neptune pieces come out byte-for-byte identical to the last edition's, because a marking here partitions a globe without moving its surface. Nothing else in the set changed.
product.title: Antisol Poseidon
product.what_arrives: Forty-two printed parts: sixteen worlds, a board in four panels, twelve asteroid-belt tiles, two stars, six corona cells and two storage trays. Nothing is glued, screwed or assembled; the tiles and stars drop into their own pockets and the panels butt together.
